A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CR-DAgger work, with readable main text and appendices. However, v3 claims evaluation on four tasks while its displayed experiments cover two; gear-insertion and cable-routing panels exist only in cropped-out figure content. This limits verification of the claimed coverage expansion.

before.justification: v2 reports original robot experiments on book flipping and belt assembly, including success rates, training ablations, stage-wise results and the base-action-input ablation.

after.justification: v3 retains original book-flipping experiments and reports revised belt-assembly results, including force-input and KL-regularized baselines.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 retain the delta-correction interface, frozen-encoder residual network, force inputs and outputs, action representation and admittance-based execution. The added controller documentation does not establish a new component; the correction-batch schedule changes are assessed under E3.

E1.justification: Both versions visibly evaluate book flipping and belt assembly; v3 adds four grasp locations to belt testing. However, its conclusion changes from two tasks to four, while gear-insertion and cable-routing results are cropped out and lack accompanying task descriptions. The full extent of added task coverage cannot be reliably established.

E2.justification: The belt comparison in Figure 6 adds a force-input base policy and KL-regularized finetuning, citing DPOK for the latter. It replaces the earlier comparison across correction interfaces with On-Policy Delta results, removing the reported Observe-then-Collect and Take-over-Correction belt comparisons. Book-flipping comparator membership is retained.

E3.justification: Belt base-policy training changes from 150 to 405 demonstrations, and evaluation increases from 20 to 32 rollouts. Section 4.5 changes belt correction training from one batch of 50 episodes to two batches of 50, while book flipping retains one batch. These materially revise the training budget and evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: v3 removes v2 Appendix A.2 and Table 1, which tested including base-policy actions as residual-policy inputs, and removes the displayed belt stage-wise analysis from Figure 8. It adds a force-input control to investigate force sensing versus human corrections and revises the belt failure cases to emphasize missed slotting and slippage. The book training-frequency and sampling ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregate success rates without training-seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The increased belt rollout count changes evaluation sample size, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 6 replaces the belt results: v2 reports 20% for the base policy and 70% for CR with On-Policy Delta; v3 reports 15.6% without force, 43.8% with force and 96.8% for CR, plus 3.1% for KL-regularized finetuning. These use changed settings and do not establish a same-setting performance gain. Book scores and Figure 7 remain unchanged; the base-action ablation and displayed belt stage-wise results disappear.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical results or proofs, and the policy notation in Figure 3 is retained. The new compliance-control appendix provides standard conceptual and implementation explanations without adding formal assumptions, definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The two central method contributions remain unchanged. The abstract and introduction raise the stated improvement from over 50% to over 60%, the introduction drops the fewer-than-50-interventions claim, and the conclusion expands its evaluation claim from two tasks to four despite only two being displayed.

C2.justification: v3 softens claims about maintaining the original policy distribution and replaces the general single-batch recommendation with task-dependent large-batch guidance. It adds the labor burden of kinesthetic teaching as a limitation and removes the appendix discussion of task-dependent benefits from base-action inputs.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.1 explains the independent control loops, discloses the 500 Hz admittance controller and hardware-driver buffering, and provides a controller-code link. The introduction replaces a future-release promise with a resource-access link. Conversely, removing v2 Appendix A.2 also removes the task-specific base-action-input choices; linked resources were not accessed.

R1.justification: v3 adds six cited works covering visual representations, KL-regularized finetuning, compliance control and active perception. The main positioning relative to DAgger and residual policy learning is retained. The Adaptive Compliance Policy reference changes publication metadata rather than identifying a new work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, with localized revisions to distribution terminology, experimental descriptions, findings and limitations. The appendix adds control-implementation and broader-impact sections and reorganizes existing material; the publication banner and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: Figure 5 replaces the belt rollout and failure photographs and adds grasp-height illustration. Figure 6 substantially revises comparator grouping, displays base policies as bars and expands the belt success-rate scale. Figure 8 is reduced from six displayed panels to three book-flipping panels, and Table 1 is removed, materially changing the presentation of experimental evidence.

improvement.justification: The force-input control, clearer implementation documentation and resource links improve attribution and reproducibility information. However, v3 removes informative ablations and belt comparisons and introduces reporting inconsistencies: the conclusion claims four tasks although only two are displayed, and Section 4.4 retains the old 50% belt gain despite revised Figure 6 results. Its stated 53% advantage also corresponds to the force-input baseline, despite describing a position-only comparison. These benefits and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain.
